title: Infraposition and Proximal Contact Loss in Implant-Supported Restorations Within Natural Dentitions: A Survey of Frequency, Mechanisms, Clinical Sequelae, and Evidence Synthesis

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Definitions
subsections.subsection_title: Definition of infraposition in implant-supported restorations
subsections.content:
Infraposition in implant-supported restorations denotes a vertical discrepancy in which the implant crown or fixed implant prosthesis becomes positioned more apically relative to adjacent natural teeth and the evolving occlusal plane over time. The phenomenon is also described in the literature as "implant infraocclusion" or "relative apical displacement," emphasizing that the implant itself usually remains osseointegrated and stationary while neighboring dentition continues eruption and alveolar development, particularly after adolescence ref [1], ref [2].

Conceptually, infraposition should be distinguished from technical or biologic complications that can also alter crown level, such as abutment screw loosening, prosthesis wear, peri-implant bone loss, or implant malposition. Infraposition is therefore best defined as a time-dependent relative vertical mismatch between an implant restoration and adjacent teeth, measured clinically or radiographically from stable reference points, rather than as true apical migration of the implant fixture itself ref [3], ref [4].

This definition is clinically important because even small vertical discrepancies may compromise esthetics, occlusal harmony, and interproximal relationships in single implants placed in partially dentate patients. Longitudinal studies and systematic reviews have shown that such relative vertical change can continue in adulthood, supporting the use of infraposition as a dynamic outcome variable in long-term assessment of implant-supported restorations adjacent to natural dentition ref [2], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Definitions
subsections.subsection_title: Definition of missing proximal contact points
subsections.content:
A missing proximal contact point (MPCP), in the context of an implant-supported restoration adjacent to natural teeth, refers to the loss or absence of the intended physical contact between the implant crown and the neighboring tooth at the interproximal aspect. Clinically, this is usually operationalized as an open contact that permits passage of dental floss without resistance or presents as a visible/measurable interproximal gap on examination, casts, or radiographs. The concept is distinct from papillary deficiency: a contact may be present while the papilla is reduced, and conversely an open contact may coexist with apparently preserved soft tissue contours ref [6], ref [7].

In implant dentistry, MPCP is most often discussed as a time-dependent complication rather than a fabrication error. Longitudinal studies have shown that proximal contacts initially established at delivery may open during function and growth-related or physiologic tooth movement, particularly on the mesial side of implant restorations adjacent to natural teeth ref [8], ref [9]. Thus, the definition should encompass both contacts that were never achieved adequately and contacts that were lost after insertion, because both scenarios create the same clinically relevant endpoint: a discontinuity in proximal support and containment.

From a clinical-outcome perspective, MPCP matters because it is associated with food impaction, patient discomfort, increased maintenance burden, and potential effects on peri-implant and periodontal health ref [8], ref [10]. For longitudinal assessment, the preferred definition is therefore pragmatic: any absent or functionally ineffective proximal contact between an implant restoration and an adjacent natural tooth, recorded at a specified follow-up interval and ideally characterized by location (mesial/distal), severity, and method of detection.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Definitions
subsections.subsection_title: Natural dentition versus ankylosed implant behavior
subsections.content:
A central biological distinction between teeth and osseointegrated implants is that natural teeth remain suspended in the periodontal ligament, whereas implants are functionally ankylosed to bone. Because the periodontal ligament permits adaptive eruption, mesial drift, and continuous compensation for occlusal wear, neighboring teeth may continue to change position throughout growth and adulthood. In contrast, an implant lacks this eruptive and migratory potential and therefore behaves as a comparatively stationary reference point once osseointegration is established ref [11], ref [12].

This difference is clinically important because craniofacial growth and dentoalveolar remodeling do not cease abruptly after adolescence. Longitudinal observations have shown continued vertical development of the alveolar process and positional changes of teeth even in adults, which can leave an implant-supported crown appearing progressively apical relative to adjacent dentition, a phenomenon often described as infraposition or relative infraocclusion ref [13], ref [14]. The same biologic mismatch also helps explain why proximal contacts next to implant restorations are vulnerable to opening over time: natural teeth may drift mesially while the implant restoration remains fixed ref [15].

Accordingly, ankylosed implant behavior should not be interpreted as pathologic in itself; rather, it reflects the absence of the adaptive mobility and eruptive capacity intrinsic to natural teeth. This conceptual contrast underpins longitudinal assessment of implant restorations in partially dentate patients, especially in younger individuals and in esthetically demanding regions where even small discrepancies in vertical level or contact relationships may become clinically significant ref [12], ref [14], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Definitions
subsections.subsection_title: Relationship between infraposition and contact point changes
subsections.content:
Infraposition and loss of proximal contact are mechanistically related but not synonymous phenomena. Infraposition describes the relative apical displacement of an implant-supported crown compared with adjacent teeth as the natural dentition continues eruptive and compensatory vertical movement while the osseointegrated implant behaves ankylotically. This vertical discrepancy alters the interproximal relationship and can contribute to an open contact, especially when accompanied by mesial drift and rotational changes of neighboring teeth rather than by prosthesis movement alone [1,2].

Clinical studies indicate that proximal contact loss is common over time around implant restorations and occurs predominantly at the mesial aspect, supporting the view that physiologic tooth migration is a major driver [3,4]. Infraposition may amplify this process by changing the vertical level at which adjacent crowns meet, reducing the area of proximal engagement and making a previously stable contact more susceptible to opening under functional wear, settling, or continued dentoalveolar adaptation. However, contact loss can also occur without clinically obvious infraposition, indicating partial overlap rather than equivalence between the two outcomes [3,5].

Conceptually, infraposition should therefore be regarded as one longitudinal dimensional change that may predispose to, but does not fully explain, proximal contact alteration. This distinction is important in study design and reporting: vertical discrepancy and contact point integrity should be measured as separate endpoints, because they reflect related yet different consequences of the mismatch between lifelong tooth movement and implant immobility [1,2,4].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Definitions
subsections.content:
The clinical expression of infraposition and loss of proximal contact is strongly conditioned by treatment setting. Most longitudinal evidence concerns single implant-supported crowns placed in partially edentulous adults and bordered by natural teeth, because this configuration most clearly exposes the contrast between continued dentoalveolar change and the relative ankylotic behavior of osseointegrated implants ref [21], ref [22]. Anterior maxillary restorations have received particular attention, as even small vertical discrepancies may become esthetically evident and may be accompanied by open contacts or altered papilla relationships over time ref [21], ref [23].

Restoration type also matters. Cement-retained and screw-retained single crowns share the same biologic susceptibility to positional discrepancy relative to adjacent teeth, but they differ in retrievability and in the ease with which contact areas can be adjusted during maintenance. In contrast, implant-supported fixed partial dentures may distribute positional changes across a larger prosthetic segment, potentially masking localized contact changes while creating more complex contact relationships at terminal abutment teeth. Clinical observations further suggest that posterior restorations are especially relevant when discussing missing proximal contacts because mesial drift and occlusal wear of neighboring teeth can progressively alter interproximal relationships despite implant stability ref [24], ref [25].

Accordingly, this survey focuses primarily on implant-supported restorations in patients with residual craniofacial growth potential or ongoing adult dentition change, especially single-tooth replacements adjacent to natural teeth. Fully edentulous implant prostheses are conceptually less informative for this question because there are no natural neighboring teeth against which infraposition or contact-point loss can be defined in the same way ref [22], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Reported frequency estimates for implant infraposition and implant-proximal missing contact points vary widely because studies differ in outcome definitions, dentition stage, and follow-up duration. For infraposition, the classic longitudinal observations in young adults showed that ankylosed implants may continue to appear submerged relative to adjacent teeth as craniofacial growth and dentoalveolar eruption persist, making the phenomenon common enough to be clinically relevant even after apparently completed growth ref [26]. A systematic review likewise concluded that vertical discrepancy is not rare, but pooled prevalence is difficult to derive because studies use different thresholds and measurement methods ref [27].

For proximal contact loss, available cohort studies suggest substantially higher occurrence than for clinically obvious infraposition. In posterior single-implant restorations, contact loss with adjacent teeth has been reported in a sizeable minority to a majority of restorations during maintenance, with mesial contacts more frequently affected than distal contacts ref [28]. A systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that open proximal contacts around implant restorations are a frequent technical-biologic complication, with prevalence increasing over time and varying by arch and contact surface ref [29].

Incidence estimates should therefore be interpreted as scenario-specific rather than universal. Studies with shorter observation periods often report early contact loss events, whereas infraposition tends to emerge cumulatively over longer follow-up and is especially emphasized in younger patients and the anterior maxilla ref [1,2,5]. This heterogeneity underscores the need for standardized case definitions when comparing epidemiologic estimates across studies.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Available longitudinal evidence indicates that both implant infraposition and loss of proximal contact tend to increase with time rather than remain static. For infraposition, early observations in single-implant restorations showed that the vertical discrepancy relative to adjacent teeth may continue for years after crown delivery, consistent with ongoing dentoalveolar change in the natural dentition while the implant remains ankylosed ref [31], ref [32]. Long-term follow-up studies similarly suggest that the phenomenon is cumulative, with larger infraocclusal discrepancies becoming more apparent at extended observation intervals, especially when restorations are placed before complete cessation of craniofacial growth ref [33].

A comparable time-dependent pattern has been reported for proximal contact loss. Cohort studies of implant-supported single crowns have shown that contact points judged acceptable at delivery are increasingly lost during follow-up, with higher frequencies at later recalls, indicating that contact deterioration is a progressive maintenance issue rather than an isolated early complication ref [34], ref [35]. This progression appears to reflect continuous mesial drift and positional change of adjacent teeth, so the risk persists even in otherwise stable osseointegrated restorations ref [34], ref [36].

Taken together, the longitudinal literature supports a model of gradual divergence between implants and the natural dentition over time. Clinically, this means that short follow-up intervals may underestimate the burden of both infraposition and contact loss, whereas studies with longer surveillance are more likely to capture cumulative expression, repeated adjustments, and the need for corrective intervention ref [32], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Age is a consistent modifier of the distribution of implant infraposition. The highest susceptibility is observed when implants are placed before completion of craniofacial growth, because osseointegrated implants behave ankylotically and do not follow continued eruption and alveolar development of adjacent teeth. This concern was established in classic analyses of implants placed in adolescents and young adults, where infraocclusion became clinically evident over time and was linked to residual vertical facial growth rather than implant failure per se ref [37], ref [38].

Importantly, the age effect is not limited to teenagers. Long-term follow-up studies have shown that continuous eruption and dentoalveolar remodeling persist into adulthood, so even implants inserted after the traditional growth period may show progressive infraposition, although the magnitude is generally smaller and the variability wider than in younger patients ref [39], ref [40]. In practice, this means that chronological adulthood lowers but does not eliminate risk, especially in patients with hyperdivergent growth patterns or ongoing occlusal change.

For missing interproximal contact points, age-related patterns are less directly studied, but the same biologic logic applies: younger patients and those with greater post-treatment tooth migration may be more prone to contact loss adjacent to implants. Reviews synthesizing longitudinal evidence therefore recommend particular caution in adolescents and young adults, and advocate delayed implant placement in esthetic regions whenever feasible until skeletal growth is demonstrably complete ref [38], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Site-specific variation is a consistent theme in reports on implant infraposition and proximal contact loss. The problem is most visible in the anterior maxilla, where continued craniofacial growth, eruption of adjacent teeth, and high esthetic sensitivity make even small vertical discrepancies clinically apparent. Long-term observational work on single implants has repeatedly shown that maxillary anterior restorations are especially prone to infraocclusion over time, particularly in younger adults and adolescents, whereas posterior sites may show less obvious esthetic manifestation even when relative vertical change occurs ref [42], ref [43].

For proximal contact loss, site effects appear to be driven less by visibility and more by post-eruptive tooth movement. Adjacent natural teeth tend to drift mesially, so missing contact points are reported more often on the mesial aspect of implant restorations than on the distal aspect. This mesial predominance has been documented in clinical follow-up studies and systematic reviews, which also suggest that posterior segments may be particularly susceptible because cumulative mesial drift and occlusal wear are more pronounced there ref [44], ref [45].

Arch-specific tendencies may also interact with site. In the maxilla, anterior esthetic demands amplify the detection of infraposition, while in the mandible and posterior regions, functional sequelae such as food impaction may be the dominant presentation of contact loss rather than visible vertical discrepancy. Overall, site-specific patterns therefore reflect a combination of growth biology, tooth migration, and restoration detectability, rather than a single uniform mechanism ref [43], ref [45], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Reported frequencies of infraposition and proximal contact loss are not uniform across prosthetic designs. Single implant-supported crowns are the restoration type most consistently associated with mesial contact loss, presumably because the implant remains ankylosed while adjacent teeth continue physiologic migration; this pattern was emphasized in longitudinal clinical studies of posterior single crowns and in systematic reviews synthesizing these cohorts ref [47], ref [48]. By contrast, splinted implant restorations and fixed partial dentures may distribute forces differently and can reduce the number of vulnerable implant-tooth interfaces, although they do not eliminate contact-related complications.

Restoration retention mode may also contribute to variation. In a retrospective study of implant prostheses, proximal contact loss and open contacts were frequent technical/biologic maintenance findings, with single-unit restorations particularly affected ref [49]. Screw-retained restorations may facilitate monitoring and correction of contact changes, whereas cement-retained designs can make repeated retrieval more difficult; however, available evidence suggests that prosthesis configuration is a stronger determinant of contact behavior than retention mode alone.

Aesthetic-zone restorations show a somewhat different profile. Infraposition has been discussed mainly for anterior implant-supported crowns placed in adolescents and young adults, where continued craniofacial growth can leave an implant crown apically displaced relative to neighboring teeth ref [50], ref [51]. Thus, restoration-specific variation reflects both prosthesis design and site-specific biology: posterior single crowns are more often linked to proximal contact loss, while anterior single crowns are the classic setting for clinically evident infraposition over time.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Longitudinal Frequency Over Time
subsections.content:
Evidence on recurrence after corrective intervention is limited, but the available literature indicates that both infraposition-related esthetic discrepancies and interproximal contact loss can reappear after treatment because the underlying mechanisms often persist. In the esthetic zone, replacement of implant crowns or soft-tissue/prosthetic modification may temporarily re-establish incisal alignment, yet continued craniofacial growth can produce renewed relative infraposition over time, particularly in younger adults and after long follow-up intervals ref [52], ref [53].

For proximal contact loss, recurrence appears especially plausible after simple chairside correction, since remesial drift of adjacent teeth is ongoing and implant ankylosis prevents physiologic adaptation of the restoration. Longitudinal studies and systematic reviews on implant contact loss consistently describe the phenomenon as progressive and time-dependent, implying that restored contacts may not remain stable without repeated maintenance ref [54], ref [55]. Clinical reports further suggest that recurrent open contacts are more frequent when the original etiologic factors—posterior tooth migration, occlusal wear, and arch changes—are not addressed by the correction strategy itself ref [56].

Taken together, recurrence should be viewed not as a rare complication of failed repair, but as an expected consequence of a dynamic dentition opposing a static implant restoration. This has epidemiologic implications: post-correction event rates are likely cumulative, and studies reporting single-time prevalence after repair may underestimate the lifetime burden of repeated interventions. Accordingly, long-term surveillance rather than one-time correction is the more realistic framework for managing these complications ref [53], ref [55], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.content:
Continued eruption and residual craniofacial growth are central biologic explanations for infraposition of ankylosed implants. Unlike natural teeth, implants lack a periodontal ligament and therefore do not participate in compensatory eruption as the dentoalveolar complex adapts to ongoing vertical facial growth and occlusal change. This concept was articulated clinically by Andersson and colleagues, who reported progressive infraocclusion of osseointegrated implants placed in adolescents, and by Thilander et al., who showed that implants behave like ankylosed units in the growing face, with increasing discrepancy relative to adjacent teeth over time [1,2].

Importantly, this mechanism is not confined to childhood. Longitudinal cephalometric work indicates that craniofacial growth, especially in the vertical dimension, can persist into early and even later adulthood, providing a biologic basis for delayed emergence of implant infraposition after apparently stable treatment [3]. Consistent with this, Bernard et al. documented continuous eruption of maxillary incisors and infraposition of adjacent implant crowns in adults over long-term follow-up, suggesting that small but cumulative dentoalveolar changes remain clinically relevant after growth completion by conventional criteria [4].

A related implication is that susceptibility is likely greater in patients with vertical growth tendencies or long-face patterns, where ongoing lower facial height increase may accentuate relative implant submergence. Although individual prediction remains imperfect, the available evidence supports viewing infraposition as a time-dependent mismatch between a static ankylosed prosthetic unit and a dynamic craniofacial system, rather than as a purely prosthetic complication [2,5].

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.subsection_title: Physiologic mesial drift of natural teeth
subsections.content:
Physiologic mesial drift is a lifelong tendency for natural teeth to migrate toward the midline, driven by remodeling of proximal and periodontal tissues under occlusal function. Classic biologic models attribute this movement to transseptal fiber tension and adaptive alveolar bone turnover, with proximal wear helping create the space that is subsequently closed by mesial migration ref [61], ref [62]. In dentitions containing implants, this normal mobility is asymmetric: ankylosed implants remain essentially stationary while adjacent teeth continue to drift, creating a plausible mechanism for progressive opening of interproximal contact points over time.

Longitudinal clinical studies support the reality of ongoing mesial migration in adulthood. Using implants as stable reference markers, investigators have shown continuous positional change of neighboring teeth after implant restoration, particularly in posterior segments, consistent with physiologic drift rather than prosthesis instability alone ref [63], ref [64]. This helps explain why contact loss may emerge even when the restoration was delivered with apparently adequate initial interproximal tightness.

From an etiologic perspective, mesial drift likely interacts with other age-related dentoalveolar processes, including occlusal wear, compensatory eruption, and periodontal ligament-mediated tooth mobility. The consequence is a dynamic natural dentition opposed to a static implant-supported crown, producing a time-dependent mismatch in tooth position. Reviews of implant contact loss have therefore identified physiologic mesial migration of adjacent teeth as one of the most consistent conceptual explanations for this complication ref [65].

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.subsection_title: Occlusal wear and vertical dentoalveolar compensation
subsections.content:
Occlusal wear is relevant to infraposition because the natural dentition can partially maintain vertical occlusal relationships through compensatory dentoalveolar eruption, whereas osseointegrated implants lack this adaptive capacity. Classic longitudinal observations showed that tooth wear is often accompanied by continuous eruption and remodeling of the alveolar process rather than a simple loss of occlusal vertical dimension, indicating that the dentition remains dynamic throughout adult life ref [66], ref [67]. In mixed-age populations, this compensatory mechanism helps preserve interarch contact despite attrition, but it may also accentuate the relative apical position of an implant-supported crown over time.

This concept is consistent with implant follow-up studies in which apparent infraocclusion has been interpreted not as implant intrusion, but as ongoing eruption of adjacent teeth and vertical growth or dentoalveolar adaptation in the surrounding dentition ref [68], ref [69]. From a mechanistic standpoint, wear-related compensation likely interacts with continued eruption, periodontal ligament function, and alveolar bone apposition around natural teeth; these processes can proceed even after facial growth is thought to be complete. Consequently, patients with substantial occlusal wear, parafunction, or age-related cumulative attrition may be especially susceptible to progressive discrepancies in incisal or occlusal level between teeth and implant restorations.

Clinically, this framework implies that infraposition risk is not determined solely by skeletal growth status at implant placement. It may also reflect the lifelong balance between occlusal wear and the capacity for vertical dentoalveolar compensation in the natural dentition, a balance from which the ankylosed implant is biologically excluded ref [67], ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.subsection_title: Periodontal ligament-mediated mobility of adjacent teeth
subsections.content:
A central biologic asymmetry between implants and neighboring teeth is the presence of the periodontal ligament (PDL) around natural teeth and its absence around osseointegrated implants. The PDL confers viscoelastic mobility and enables continuous adaptive remodeling in response to occlusal loading and altered interproximal forces, whereas implants behave as ankylosed units. This difference has long been recognized as a source of divergent movement patterns under function and over time, helping explain why adjacent teeth may continue to migrate while the implant-supported crown remains stationary, predisposing to loss of proximal contact and apparent infraposition relative to the natural dentition ref [71], ref [72].

Experimental and clinical studies show that natural teeth exhibit axial and lateral displacement under load because of PDL deformation, with recovery after unloading, while implants display much smaller movement amplitudes and different force transmission characteristics ref [73], ref [74]. In the interproximal dimension, these PDL-mediated tooth movements interact with mesial drift and occlusal adaptation, so that neighboring teeth can progressively change position independently of the restoration. Longitudinal observations of implant restorations have therefore reported open proximal contacts as a frequent complication, particularly on the mesial side, consistent with continued physiologic mobility of adjacent teeth rather than migration of the implant itself ref [75], ref [76].

Conceptually, PDL-mediated mobility should be viewed not as an isolated mechanism but as an enabling substrate that amplifies age-related tooth migration, wear-related compensation, and occlusal disequilibrium. Its relevance is greatest where interproximal stability depends on a rigid implant contact against a tooth that retains lifelong eruptive and positional responsiveness.

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.content:
Patient-level risk appears to reflect the balance between lifelong dentofacial change and the relative ankylosis of osseointegrated implants. Younger age at implant placement is consistently discussed as a major susceptibility factor because residual craniofacial growth and post-adolescent vertical development can continue into adulthood, increasing the likelihood that adjacent teeth erupt or migrate relative to the implant restoration. Long-term observations of single implants in the anterior maxilla have shown that infraposition is more frequent and more pronounced in younger patients and in those followed over longer periods ref [77], ref [78].

Sex may also modify risk, likely through differences in timing and duration of craniofacial growth. In a systematic review of infraocclusion of implant-supported restorations, male sex and placement in younger individuals were recurrently identified as possible risk indicators, although the strength of evidence remained limited by heterogeneous study designs ref [79]. More broadly, longitudinal cephalometric work demonstrates that vertical facial growth and dentoalveolar eruption continue well beyond adolescence, providing a biologic rationale for patient-specific variation in implant-tooth discrepancy over time ref [80].

Other patient-level characteristics are plausible but less firmly established. Individuals with hyperdivergent facial patterns, ongoing occlusal wear, parafunctional loading, or periodontal susceptibility may experience greater compensatory eruption or tooth migration, thereby increasing the risk of open contacts or relative infraposition. However, these factors remain incompletely quantified in implant-specific cohorts, and current evidence supports viewing patient age, growth status, and duration of follow-up as the most reproducible patient-related predictors ref [79], ref [81].

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.content:
Implant- and prosthesis-related variables are plausible modifiers of both infraposition and loss of proximal contact because osseointegrated implants behave as ankylosed units, whereas adjacent teeth retain periodontal ligament-mediated mobility. Long-term cohort data indicate that marginal bone level changes around implants are usually modest after initial remodeling, yet vertical discrepancies may still accumulate clinically because the implant-supported crown does not participate in continued dentoalveolar adaptation of neighboring teeth ref [82], ref [83]. This conceptual mismatch is most relevant in younger adults, but it may persist throughout adulthood when natural teeth continue to erupt or migrate mesially.

Prosthetic design may further influence contact stability. In a prospective clinical study, loss of proximal contact was common at implant restorations, especially on the mesial side, supporting the view that contact opening reflects ongoing physiologic tooth migration against a relatively immobile implant crown ref [84]. Contact behavior can also be affected by restoration contour, crown emergence profile, and interproximal morphology, which determine the initial tightness and the capacity to accommodate small positional changes without creating a clinically detectable gap. Screw-retained versus cement-retained retention may be less important biologically than whether the prosthesis permits precise, durable contact adjustment over time.

Implant position is another treatment-related determinant. Placement that is too distal, too palatal/lingual, or otherwise discordant with the natural tooth axis may alter occlusal loading, proximal contact geometry, and embrasure form, thereby increasing susceptibility to food impaction and contact loss. These concerns parallel consensus recommendations that implant positioning and prosthetic planning should be restoration-driven and should respect peri-implant tissue dimensions and neighboring root anatomy ref [85], ref [86]. Thus, implant restorations should be viewed not as static replacements but as fixed elements inserted into a biologically dynamic dentition.

subsections.section_title: Etiological Mechanisms and Risk Factors
subsections.content:
Local anatomy and implant position plausibly modulate both infraposition and loss of proximal contact by altering how surrounding teeth continue to erupt, drift, and remodel while the implant remains ankylosed. Clinical studies of single implants in the anterior maxilla show that infraocclusion is more evident when implants are placed in sites subject to ongoing vertical dentoalveolar change and high esthetic scrutiny, particularly in younger patients and in positions with a high smile line or thin peri-implant soft tissues, where even small discrepancies become clinically apparent ref [87], ref [15].

Mesiodistal location also matters. Contact loss has been reported more frequently on the mesial side of implant restorations, consistent with the direction of physiologic tooth migration, but site-specific anatomy may amplify this tendency. Arch form, interdental spacing, angulation of adjacent roots, and the presence of tapered crowns can reduce the area and stability of the contact zone, making small positional changes clinically relevant. In posterior regions, differences in occlusal loading and cusp-fossa relationships may further influence the expression of contact opening around implant crowns ref [25], ref [88].

Buccolingual and apicocoronal implant placement are additional determinants because they constrain emergence profile and contact geometry. Excessively facial or shallow placement can force overcontoured crowns with narrower or more incisally/occlusally positioned contact areas, potentially reducing resistance to adjacent-tooth drift and increasing food impaction risk. Consensus recommendations for implant positioning in the esthetic zone therefore emphasize three-dimensional placement relative to adjacent teeth and the alveolar envelope, not only for soft-tissue preservation but also for maintaining stable interproximal relationships over time ref [85], ref [89].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical detection of proximal contact loss
subsections.content:
Clinical detection of proximal contact loss (PCL) around implant-supported restorations is usually based on direct chairside assessment of the interproximal relationship between the implant crown and the adjacent natural tooth. In practice, studies have most often operationalized PCL as the ability to pass dental floss through the contact without resistance, sometimes supplemented by patient-reported food impaction or by visual confirmation of an open contact ref [90], ref [91]. Because implant restorations lack physiologic mesial drift and periodontal ligament-mediated tooth movement, clinical examination should consider that a previously acceptable contact may open over time even in the absence of obvious prosthetic complications ref [92], ref [93].

Methodologically, floss-based detection is attractive because it is inexpensive and easily repeatable, but its diagnostic threshold is not uniform across studies. Some protocols classify any freely passing floss as PCL, whereas others distinguish between tight, light, or absent resistance, creating heterogeneity in reported prevalence. This is important because food impaction and patient discomfort correlate more strongly with clinically perceptible loss of contact than with subtle variations in contact tightness alone ref [91], ref [94]. Standardized recording should therefore specify the floss type, direction of passage, examiner calibration, and whether the finding is unilateral or bilateral.

From a clinical surveillance perspective, PCL is best assessed longitudinally at routine maintenance visits and interpreted alongside symptoms, peri-implant tissue status, and occlusal/prosthetic integrity. Prospective implant cohort studies have shown that open contacts are common over time and may require periodic adjustment or restoration remake ref [90], ref [93], ref [48]. A purely binary diagnosis may underestimate progression; documenting contact status serially improves comparability across studies and helps distinguish transient contact changes from persistent, clinically relevant PCL.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Radiographic and photographic evaluation of infraposition
subsections.content:
Radiographic and photographic methods are central to documenting infraposition because the phenomenon is fundamentally relative: the implant-supported crown remains static while adjacent dentition and alveolar processes continue vertical development or remodeling. Serial standardized intraoral photographs can reveal progressive incisal or occlusal step formation, especially in the anterior maxilla, whereas periapical radiographs are more useful when calibrated to stable reference points such as adjacent cemento-enamel junctions, implant platform position, or crown margins. Early longitudinal studies of single implants in young adults relied on repeated clinical photographs and radiographs to demonstrate that vertical discrepancy may increase over time even when implants remain osseointegrated and otherwise successful clinically ref [95], ref [96].

Methodological rigor is critical because apparent infraposition is highly sensitive to projection geometry, magnification, and changes in head posture. Standardized long-cone periapical imaging with individualized holders improves reproducibility, but two-dimensional radiographs cannot fully capture facial or palatal displacement components and may underestimate esthetic consequences. For this reason, several authors have emphasized combining radiographic assessment with frontal and lateral photographic records, often using neighboring natural teeth as internal controls and measuring vertical discrepancy from reproducible coronal landmarks ref [97], ref [98]. In long-term follow-up studies, photographic evaluation has been particularly informative for visible anterior changes, whereas radiographs remain necessary to distinguish true infraposition from crown wear, eruption of adjacent teeth, or prosthetic replacement effects ref [96], ref [99].

Three-dimensional imaging has theoretical advantages, but routine CBCT use for isolated infraposition monitoring is constrained by radiation exposure and limited evidence for superior longitudinal precision in this indication. Accordingly, most studies continue to treat standardized photography and calibrated intraoral radiography as the practical reference methods, while acknowledging that differences in image standardization partly explain between-study variation in reported prevalence and severity of infraposition ref [97], ref [99], ref [100].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.content:
Quantitative definitions of infraposition and proximal contact loss (PCL) vary substantially across studies, which complicates prevalence estimates and interstudy comparison. For infraposition, most clinical reports operationalize the condition as a vertical discrepancy between the implant crown and adjacent teeth measured clinically, photographically, or radiographically, but the threshold used to define a clinically relevant event ranges from barely perceptible change to approximately 1 mm. Long-term observational work on single implants in the anterior maxilla helped normalize the use of millimeter-based thresholds by documenting progressive infraocclusion over time and emphasizing that even modest vertical discrepancies may become esthetically relevant in young adults ref [101], ref [102].

For PCL, grading systems are often binary at the point of examination (contact present/absent), typically using dental floss resistance as the diagnostic threshold; however, some authors further distinguish unilateral versus bilateral loss, spontaneous versus recurrent loss, and the need for restorative intervention. This simplification improves feasibility in longitudinal studies but obscures severity, because a floss-pass criterion does not capture contact tightness, food impaction frequency, or patient burden. Reviews of implant complications have therefore highlighted the need for standardized case definitions that separate simple contact opening from clinically consequential PCL associated with food impaction, tissue inflammation, or repeated maintenance requirements ref [36], ref [103].

A pragmatic grading framework should therefore combine an objective threshold with a consequence-based modifier: for infraposition, absolute vertical discrepancy (for example, <1 mm vs. ≥1 mm) together with esthetic visibility; for PCL, contact status together with symptomatology and retreatment frequency. Such multidimensional grading is more consistent with the biology of continuous tooth eruption and mesial drift around osseointegrated implants and may improve comparability across future cohort studies and trials ref [102], ref [104].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.content:
Longitudinal follow-up protocols are central because both implant infraposition and proximal contact loss are time-dependent phenomena that may emerge only after the initial restorative phase. Across prospective and retrospective cohorts, assessments are typically anchored to crown delivery or definitive prosthesis insertion and then repeated at regular intervals, most commonly annually, to capture gradual vertical discrepancy and contact changes under continuing craniofacial growth and adjacent tooth migration ref [101], ref [105]. This design choice is particularly important in younger adults, in whom small yearly changes can accumulate into clinically visible esthetic or functional discrepancies over longer observation periods.

Methodologically, protocols with standardized serial periapical radiographs and calibrated clinical examinations are more informative than cross-sectional reassessment alone. Long-term implant studies in the anterior maxilla have shown that meaningful vertical change may only become evident after 5 years or more, supporting extended recall windows rather than short postrestorative surveillance ref [101], ref [106]. For proximal contact loss, repeated chairside evaluation using floss resistance, shimstock, or direct inspection at multiple recall visits is preferable, since contact status may fluctuate and differs by mesial versus distal surface and by opposing dentition over time ref [107], ref [9].

For comparability across studies, follow-up protocols should report the observation start point, recall interval, total duration, attrition, and whether measurements are referenced to adjacent teeth, stable skeletal landmarks, or serial casts/digital models. Heterogeneous timing and inconsistent endpoints remain a major source of between-study variability, especially when outcomes are dichotomized at the final visit rather than modeled as trajectories ref [105], ref [9], ref [108].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.content:
Reliability is a central concern in studies of infraposition and proximal contact loss because the detected changes are often small and accumulate gradually over time. Measurement error can arise from projection geometry, head positioning, magnification, landmark selection, and the choice of reference structures on serial radiographs or photographs. In implant research more broadly, standardized radiographic acquisition with individualized holders and calibration against known dimensions has been emphasized as a prerequisite for reproducible longitudinal comparisons, particularly when submillimeter vertical changes are being interpreted ref [109], ref [110].

For proximal contact loss, reproducibility is also influenced by how contact status is operationalized. Binary chairside detection with floss or metal strips is clinically practical, but agreement depends on the force applied and whether the endpoint is “passage,” “resistance,” or visible separation. By contrast, study models and digital scans can improve repeatability by allowing repeated inspection and metric assessment, although scanner resolution, segmentation, and superimposition protocols introduce their own sources of variability. The broader dental literature on intraoral and cast scanning shows that trueness and precision are sufficient for monitoring small dimensional changes only when acquisition protocols are tightly standardized ref [111], ref [112].

Accordingly, reports should distinguish intra-examiner repeatability from inter-examiner reproducibility and present appropriate statistics such as intraclass correlation coefficients, kappa values, or method-error analyses. For radiographic linear measurements, duplicate readings and Bland-Altman style assessment of agreement are preferable to simple correlation. Consensus statements on clinical research methods around osseointegrated implants have likewise stressed examiner calibration, blinded reassessment, and explicit error reporting to improve comparability across studies evaluating biologic and prosthetic outcomes ref [113], ref [114].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches, Measurement Protocols, and Outcome Assessment
subsections.content:
Patient-centered outcome assessment is essential because infraposition and proximal contact loss may be clinically detectable long before they are perceived as problematic by patients. In implant dentistry, esthetic appraisal has therefore increasingly incorporated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), particularly for visible anterior restorations, where dissatisfaction may arise from subtle asymmetry, papilla loss, or perceived “shortening” of the implant crown relative to adjacent teeth. Reviews of esthetic outcomes consistently emphasize that professional ratings and patient judgments are related but not interchangeable, supporting the inclusion of structured PROMs alongside clinical and radiographic measures ref [115], ref [116].

For this topic, the most relevant patient-centered domains are satisfaction with appearance, awareness of food impaction, phonetic disturbance, cleansability, and the social impact of visible discrepancy. Instruments used in implant studies have often been study-specific visual analogue scales or Likert ratings, whereas broader oral-health quality-of-life tools such as the OHIP can capture functional and psychosocial consequences when contact loss leads to packing or discomfort ref [117]. In esthetic zones, pink and white esthetic scores were originally developed as professional indices, but they are often paired with patient satisfaction scales to provide a more complete picture of treatment success ref [118].

Methodologically, patient-centered assessment should be longitudinal, because adaptation and expectations change over time and may diverge from objective progression of infraposition. Standardized questioning at baseline and follow-up, ideally with predefined thresholds for clinically important dissatisfaction or food impaction, would improve comparability across studies. This approach is consistent with broader calls to prioritize PROMs and patient preferences in implant outcome assessment rather than relying exclusively on survival or clinician-centered esthetic judgments ref [119].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.content:
Infraposition and loss of proximal contact around implant restorations have immediate functional consequences because implants do not erupt or adapt with adjacent teeth. As neighboring teeth continue physiologic eruption and mesial drift, interproximal relationships may open, creating food-trap sites and altered occlusal relationships that patients often perceive as chewing discomfort rather than frank pain ref [120], ref [9]. Clinical studies of single-implant crowns have consistently shown that proximal contact loss is common, particularly on the mesial aspect, and is frequently associated with food impaction during function ref [9], ref [121].

The hygienic burden is equally important. Open contacts and step discrepancies caused by infraposition favor retention of food debris and plaque, making routine flossing less effective and often prompting repeated use of interdental aids. In observational studies, patients with implant-supported restorations and proximal contact loss reported increased food impaction and cleaning difficulty, findings that align with the broader prosthodontic literature identifying deficient proximal contacts as a major local factor for stagnation areas and patient dissatisfaction ref [121], ref [122].

These functional and hygienic effects are not trivial, because persistent food impaction may trigger recurrent soft-tissue soreness, halitosis, and repeated emergency visits for debridement or contact adjustment. Accordingly, contact stability should be viewed not only as a prosthetic design issue but also as a determinant of day-to-day oral function and self-care around implant restorations ref [120], ref [123].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.content:
Esthetic concerns are often the first patient-perceived consequence of implant infraposition and proximal contact loss, particularly in the anterior maxilla where small discrepancies are highly visible. Because osseointegrated implants do not erupt with adjacent dentition, continued dentoalveolar development and vertical changes of neighboring teeth can leave the implant crown in relative infraocclusion, producing incisal step defects, altered gingival symmetry, and disharmony of the smile line ref [124], ref [125]. These changes may become more pronounced over time in younger adults and in patients with a high smile line, making otherwise functionally acceptable restorations esthetically unacceptable.

Loss of proximal contact also has important esthetic effects. Open contacts favor food impaction, but they also promote loss or flattening of the interproximal papilla, creating visible 'black triangles' that compromise the continuity of the anterior dentition ref [126]. In implant dentistry, papillary fill is strongly influenced by the vertical relationship between the contact point and the crestal bone; when this relationship is unfavorable, complete papilla presence becomes less predictable and esthetic deficiency is more likely ref [127]. Consequently, even minor contact migration or papilla loss around implants may disproportionately affect patient satisfaction.

These esthetic sequelae are not merely technical observations; they are closely linked to patient-reported outcomes. Objective esthetic indices for single-implant crowns, including the Pink Esthetic Score/White Esthetic Score framework, explicitly incorporate soft-tissue contour, papillae, and crown level because these features dominate lay and professional judgments of success ref [128]. Thus, prevention and early correction of infraposition and contact loss are central to maintaining long-term esthetic stability, especially in visible zones.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.content:
Loss of proximal contact adjacent to implant restorations has important periodontal and peri-implant ramifications because it promotes food impaction, plaque stagnation, and difficulty with interdental cleaning. Clinical studies have shown that open contacts next to implant-supported crowns are common over time and are frequently associated with patient-reported food impaction and increased local inflammation, even when implants themselves remain osseointegrated ref [129], ref [130]. This is biologically plausible because implants lack the periodontal ligament and do not participate in the same adaptive proximal wear and mesial drift patterns as natural teeth.

At the peri-implant level, persistent plaque retention around an open contact may aggravate bleeding on probing, peri-implant mucositis, and marginal bone loss risk, particularly in patients with limited hygiene access or a history of periodontitis. Consensus and epidemiologic data indicate that plaque accumulation and previous periodontal disease are major determinants of peri-implant inflammatory breakdown, underscoring why contact stability is not merely a prosthetic issue but also a soft- and hard-tissue maintenance issue ref [131], ref [132]. The problem may be amplified when infraposition creates step deformities and cleansability challenges in the interproximal area.

From a periodontal perspective, altered proximal architecture also affects papilla support and the biologic conditions for interproximal tissue fill. Classic work showed that the distance from the contact point to the crestal bone strongly influences papilla presence around teeth, and similar dimensional constraints are relevant when evaluating implant-adjacent embrasures ref [126]. Accordingly, surveillance of contact integrity, reinforcement of interdental hygiene, and early correction of food-trapping sites should be considered part of peri-implant disease prevention rather than deferred as minor maintenance.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Impact on prosthetic integrity and maintenance burden
subsections.content:
Loss of proximal contact and progressive infraposition increase the maintenance burden of implant-supported prostheses by creating altered loading patterns, food impaction, and recurrent patient complaints that often necessitate repeated adjustment of the restoration. Clinical follow-up studies have shown that proximal contact loss adjacent to implant restorations is common over time, particularly mesially, making it a frequent source of unscheduled maintenance and remakes rather than a trivial occlusal finding ref [133], ref [9].

From a prosthetic standpoint, continued relative vertical discrepancy can compromise occlusal harmony and the morphology of interproximal and occlusal surfaces, forcing repeated polishing, addition of restorative material, or crown replacement. Long-term evaluations of single implants in the anterior maxilla have demonstrated that infraocclusion and soft-tissue level changes continue after delivery, with consequences for esthetic integration and restoration longevity ref [120]. Similarly, studies of implant-supported crowns have linked the absence of stable proximal contacts to technical maintenance demands because contact correction may be transient when the underlying tooth movement persists ref [133], ref [134].

These problems are clinically relevant because technical complications in implant prosthodontics are cumulative: screw loosening, veneer or ceramic complications, and restorative replacement are more likely when prostheses require recurrent modification or function in a changing dentition. Reviews of implant prosthetic complications consistently identify maintenance as a central component of care, underscoring that infraposition and contact loss should be viewed not only as biologic or esthetic issues, but also as determinants of prosthetic service life and cost of care ref [135], ref [136].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.content:
Preventive treatment planning should begin with explicit recognition that osseointegrated implants do not follow the continuous eruption and dentoalveolar compensation seen in natural dentition; consequently, patients with residual craniofacial growth, marked vertical growth tendency, or long expected follow-up are at greater risk of future infraposition and contact loss. This principle is particularly important in adolescents and young adults, for whom delayed implant placement or interim tooth-borne/restorable solutions may be preferable until growth is sufficiently stable ref [137], ref [138].

Risk reduction also depends on site- and prosthesis-specific planning. Interproximal relationships should be designed to facilitate cleansability and allow future maintenance, while occlusal schemes should minimize non-axial overload and accommodate anticipated tooth movement over time. In the esthetic zone, clinicians should counsel patients that even successful implants may become relatively infraoccluded or display altered gingival relationships during long-term follow-up, especially in younger patients ref [51], ref [139].

A preventive strategy therefore combines careful timing of treatment, documentation of growth status, selection of conservative provisional options when indicated, and structured long-term review of occlusion and proximal contacts. Longitudinal observations of implant crowns adjacent to natural teeth support periodic monitoring because contact changes are common and often increase with time, making early detection central to reducing biologic and prosthetic sequelae ref [140], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Corrective management of proximal contact loss
subsections.content:
Corrective management of implant proximal contact loss is guided by symptoms, hygiene access, esthetic impact, and whether the discrepancy reflects tooth movement rather than prosthesis misfit. Because mesial drift of adjacent teeth is a dominant mechanism, recurrence after repair is common and should be discussed with patients at the outset ref [141], ref [142]. Initial management usually involves clinical and radiographic verification of the contact discrepancy, assessment of food impaction and papillary changes, and evaluation of occlusal factors or retainer loss that may be permitting tooth migration.

When the implant restoration is screw-retained or otherwise retrievable, the least invasive correction is often laboratory or chairside modification of the prosthesis to re-establish a broader, tighter contact area; this may include adding restorative material, remaking the crown, or redesigning contours to improve cleansability while avoiding excessive pressure on the neighboring tooth. In a retrospective series, interproximal contact repair commonly required replacement or modification of the implant restoration, underscoring the maintenance burden associated with this complication ref [143]. If the adjacent tooth has drifted or rotated materially, prosthesis adjustment alone may be unstable, and orthodontic repositioning or long-term retention may be necessary to restore and preserve contact relationships ref [144].

Corrective care should also address sequelae. Open contacts associated with food impaction have been linked to greater peri-implant mucosal inflammation and probing depths, so repair is not merely a comfort issue ref [145]. In selected patients with repeated recurrence, clinicians may favor restorations designed for retrievability, closer maintenance intervals, and, where appropriate, adjunctive orthodontic retention or occlusal stabilization to reduce future contact loss ref [141], ref [144].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Consequences and Management Strategies
subsections.content:
Management of implant infraposition is guided primarily by patient age, esthetic risk, and the magnitude and progression of the discrepancy. Because residual craniofacial growth can continue into adulthood, prevention centers on delaying implant placement in the anterior maxilla until growth is complete, with serial clinical and radiographic follow-up when uncertainty remains ref [146], ref [147]. In younger patients, tooth-borne or removable provisional solutions are therefore often preferred until skeletal maturation is more predictable.

When infraposition is mild and function is acceptable, monitoring or minimally invasive prosthetic compensation may be sufficient. Options include crown replacement with altered cervical contours or incisal length, though this approach is constrained by soft-tissue architecture and may camouflage rather than correct the vertical discrepancy ref [148]. In esthetically demanding sites or when the implant appears increasingly apical relative to adjacent teeth, definitive correction is more difficult because osseointegrated implants do not erupt with the dentition.

Corrective strategies range from surgical and prosthetic revision to implant removal and site redevelopment. Segmental osteotomy with coronal repositioning of the implant-bone block has been described for selected cases, but morbidity and technique sensitivity limit routine use ref [149]. More commonly, severe infraposition is managed by explantation, hard- and soft-tissue reconstruction, and replacement with a new implant or alternative prosthesis positioned to the matured dentofacial relationship ref [147], ref [150]. Thus, management is best viewed as a continuum from growth-aware prevention to individualized revision in established cases.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
The evidence base on infraposition and missing proximal contact points is dominated by observational designs, particularly retrospective cohort studies and cross-sectional follow-up series from specialist or university settings. This design landscape reflects the practical difficulty of prospectively tracking implant-supported restorations through craniofacial growth and long-term occlusal change. Classic longitudinal observational work established that continuous eruption of adjacent teeth and vertical facial growth can leave osseointegrated implants in apparent infraocclusion over time, even in adults ref [151], ref [26]. Most subsequent studies have therefore emphasized frequency estimation and descriptive risk-factor exploration rather than causal inference.

A second characteristic is the coexistence of mechanistic and clinical follow-up traditions. Cephalometric and growth-oriented studies have focused on vertical discrepancy and timing of implant placement relative to skeletal maturation ref [151], whereas prosthodontic and periodontal cohorts have concentrated on interproximal contact loss between implant restorations and neighboring teeth during maintenance follow-up ref [152], ref [88]. These studies vary markedly in unit of analysis (patient, implant, restoration, or contact surface), follow-up interval, and outcome definition, limiting direct comparability and often precluding robust pooling.

Systematic reviews consistently note that randomized trials are essentially absent, and that available studies are vulnerable to selection effects, inconsistent measurement, and incomplete control of patient age, jaw location, and restoration type ref [153], ref [27]. Accordingly, the current study design landscape is best understood as a heterogeneous observational literature that is useful for signal detection and hypothesis generation, but still insufficient for high-certainty estimates of incidence, predictors, and patient-relevant consequences.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Sources of heterogeneity in reported outcomes
subsections.content:
Reported frequencies of infraposition and open or missing proximal contact points vary widely because studies often pool biologically distinct situations. Heterogeneity arises from differences in patient age and craniofacial growth status, since continued eruption of adjacent teeth and vertical alveolar development are major determinants of relative implant infraposition after ankylotic fixation of the implant restoration ref [154], ref [155]. Estimates also differ according to site-specific growth patterns, with anterior maxillary implants typically showing greater esthetic susceptibility than posterior sites, and according to whether single implants, implant-supported crowns adjacent to natural teeth, or tooth-supported restorations are analyzed together ref [154], ref [156].

Methodological variability further amplifies between-study inconsistency. Definitions of the outcome differ: some investigators measure infraposition as any detectable vertical discrepancy, whereas others apply thresholds in millimeters or classify only clinically visible esthetic change; similarly, proximal contact loss may be defined by floss passage, shimstock, radiographic evidence, or patient-reported food impaction ref [156], ref [157]. Follow-up duration is another major source of dispersion because both infraocclusion and contact loss are time-dependent phenomena, and cross-sectional snapshots are not directly comparable with longitudinal cumulative incidence estimates ref [157], ref [158].

Additional heterogeneity reflects prosthetic and occlusal factors that are inconsistently reported, including implant-abutment connection, retention type, restoration contour, adjacent tooth mobility, periodontal support, and arch location. In reviews of implant contact loss, variation in jaw, mesial versus distal surfaces, and whether contact changes are recorded at crown delivery or after maintenance visits materially affects pooled estimates ref [157], ref [158]. Collectively, these differences mean that apparent disagreement across studies often reflects non-equivalent populations, outcome definitions, and observation windows rather than true biological contradiction.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Risk of bias in the literature on infraposition and missing proximal contact points is driven primarily by observational designs, selective sampling, and inconsistent outcome ascertainment. Most reports are retrospective case series or cross-sectional cohorts from specialist settings, which are vulnerable to selection bias and limited external validity. In addition, inadequate description of eligibility criteria, losses to follow-up, and examiner calibration weakens confidence in estimated frequencies and associations, particularly where longitudinal eruption-related changes are inferred from single time-point assessments ref [159], ref [160].

Confounding is a central concern because both infraposition and open contacts are influenced by age-related craniofacial growth, vertical skeletal pattern, implant timing, neighboring tooth eruption, and prosthetic design. Without explicit control for growth status, site, arch, and restoration characteristics, apparent effects attributed to implants or contact loss may partly reflect normal dentoalveolar development or differential loading environments. The broader epidemiologic literature on observational dental studies also underscores the need to distinguish prognostic factors from treatment effects and to address baseline imbalances analytically rather than descriptively ref [161], ref [162].

For evidence synthesis, structured bias appraisal should therefore prioritize confounding, participant selection, outcome measurement, and missing data. ROBINS-I provides a useful framework for non-randomized studies, while transparent reporting of exposure definition, follow-up intervals, and repeated contact measurements would improve causal interpretation and comparability across studies ref [163], ref [160].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Meta-analytic considerations for pooled frequency estimates
subsections.content:
Pooling frequency estimates for infraposition or missing proximal contact points requires methods tailored to proportions rather than conventional effect sizes. Because reported prevalences may approach 0 or 1 and often arise from modest single-center samples, variance stabilization and appropriate random-effects modeling are critical; commonly used options include generalized linear mixed models or transformed-proportion approaches, with the latter requiring careful interpretation at extreme values ref [164], ref [165]. In this literature, simple inverse-variance pooling is particularly vulnerable to distorted weights when event counts are sparse or when studies report multiple implants per patient without accounting for clustering.

Substantial between-study heterogeneity should be anticipated and quantified beyond a single I2 value. Differences in outcome definition, unit of analysis, follow-up interval, implant system, adjacent-tooth status, and age at placement can generate genuine dispersion in observed frequencies, making prediction intervals more informative than pooled means alone ref [166]. When enough studies are available, subgroup analysis or meta-regression should examine whether frequencies differ by skeletal maturity, anterior versus posterior sites, or whether contact loss and infraocclusion were assessed clinically versus radiographically.

Methodological rigor in prevalence reviews also depends on appraisal of bias specific to observational studies and on transparent handling of zero-event studies, duplicate cohorts, and non-independence among multiple implants from the same sample ref [167], ref [168]. For this topic, sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk studies and analyses restricted to patient-level data would likely yield more clinically interpretable pooled estimates than implant-level summaries alone.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Standardization needs in terminology and reporting
subsections.content:
A major barrier to evidence synthesis is inconsistent terminology. Studies variably label the same clinical phenomenon as infraposition, infraocclusion, submerged tooth, ankylosed primary molar, or incomplete eruption, while "missing contact point" is often conflated with open contact, contact loss, or food-impaction–prone spacing. Existing literature on infraocclusion has long emphasized the need to distinguish clinical appearance from presumed etiology, particularly because infraocclusion may be observed with or without demonstrable ankylosis ref [169], ref [170]. Without harmonized case definitions, pooled estimates inevitably mix biologically distinct entities and blur interpretation.

Reporting standards should therefore specify: tooth type and arch; developmental stage and age at diagnosis; method of ascertainment (clinical examination, study casts, bitewing or panoramic imaging); explicit severity thresholds; and whether the diagnosis reflects vertical discrepancy relative to adjacent marginal ridges, occlusal plane, or alveolar growth expectation. The use of graded severity systems in classic epidemiologic work on infraoccluded primary molars illustrates how frequency estimates depend strongly on operational definitions ref [171]. Comparable standardization is needed for contact-point outcomes, including the surface involved, timing after restoration, and whether contact was assessed qualitatively or with calibrated measures.

Greater consistency is also needed in reporting contextual variables that modify risk and prognosis, such as agenesis of the permanent successor, signs of ankylosis, craniofacial pattern, restorative material, and follow-up duration. Guidance from observational reporting frameworks can support this effort by improving transparency in eligibility criteria, measurement methods, and handling of missing data ref [172], while core outcome set methodology offers a pathway toward consensus-based endpoint selection in dental research ref [173]. A minimum reporting set would substantially improve comparability across studies and strengthen future meta-analyses.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A central unresolved controversy is whether infraposition of implant-supported crowns should be regarded primarily as a biologic inevitability of continued craniofacial growth or as a complication whose magnitude depends mainly on local restorative, occlusal, and positional factors. Long-term observational data indicate that vertical discrepancy may continue to accumulate even in adults after growth is considered complete, but the extent and clinical significance remain highly variable across studies, and thresholds for intervention are poorly defined ref [174], ref [175].

A second knowledge gap concerns the relationship between infraposition and loss of proximal contact. Distal contact loss adjacent to implant restorations is frequently reported, yet it is still unclear whether this phenomenon reflects the same underlying dentoalveolar remodeling that drives infraposition, or whether it is predominantly mediated by mesial drift, occlusal loading, arch-specific mechanics, and prosthetic design. Existing retrospective studies suggest multifactorial causation, but they do not establish temporality or quantify the contribution of patient-level modifiers such as age, sex, facial growth pattern, or parafunction ref [25], ref [15].

There is also no consensus on the most appropriate outcome metric: some authors emphasize absolute vertical step, others use radiographic or cast-based surrogates, and definitions of "contact loss" vary from floss passage to clinically visible spacing. This lack of conceptual and measurement standardization limits causal inference and impedes pooled analysis. Future research should prioritize prospective cohorts with repeated three-dimensional measurements and harmonized endpoint definitions, building on the broader consensus that implant placement in the anterior maxilla remains biologically vulnerable to ongoing postadolescent change ref [176].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Synthesis, Methodological Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Future directions for longitudinal and translational research
subsections.content:
Future longitudinal work should move beyond cross-sectional prevalence estimates and establish prospective cohorts that begin before eruption of the mixed dentition, with repeated three-dimensional assessment of vertical tooth position, contact-point development, occlusal function, and craniofacial growth. Such designs are needed to distinguish transient developmental variation from persistent infraposition and to identify time-dependent predictors, including ankylosis, local eruption disturbance, and changes in adjacent teeth. Earlier consensus work on infraocclusion highlighted the need for standardized diagnostic thresholds and timing of observation, while classic longitudinal observations suggest that severity may progress with growth rather than remain static ref [1], ref [2].

A translational priority is to connect phenotyping with mechanism. Reviews of primary failure of eruption and eruption disorders indicate that clinically similar presentations may arise from biologically distinct pathways, including ankylosis-related remodeling failure and genetically mediated eruption defects ref [3]. Integrating serial imaging with molecular and genetic data—especially in patients with familial patterns or multiple affected teeth—could clarify whether missing contact points and infraposition represent shared downstream consequences of different eruption phenotypes. Human observational studies should therefore be linked to experimental models of tooth eruption and alveolar bone adaptation, which remain central to mechanistic interpretation ref [4].

Future studies should also evaluate patient-centered and treatment-relevant outcomes: space loss, tipping of adjacent teeth, periodontal consequences, restorative burden, and quality of life. Because management ranges from monitoring to extraction, build-up, luxation, or orthodontic space management, pragmatic multicenter registries with harmonized outcome sets would improve causal inference and permit comparative effectiveness analyses. The broader framework for developing core outcome sets in clinical research offers a useful template for this field ref [5].
